body: Young Buffett's edge was huge amounts of reading (whole manuals of tiny, ignored securities), applied to very small sums where obscure net-nets and special situations were available, under a fee structure with no management fee. Later Berkshire's edge changed into roughly 1.6–1.7x leverage at below-T-bill cost (insurance float plus AAA debt), applied to cheap, safe, high-quality stocks and held for decades. Most of his dollar wealth came from that late compounding, not from the famous early trades.

body:
- Paradox of skill: Ted Williams' .406 in 1941 was about 4 standard deviations above average. A 4-sigma hitter in 2011 would bat about .380, because overall skill rose and the variance shrank. — [Advisor Perspectives (Mauboussin interview)](https://www.advisorperspectives.com/articles/2012/12/11/luck-versus-skill-in-investing-new-insights-from-the-world-of-sports-and-beyond)
- The standard deviation of mutual-fund excess returns declined steadily from 1962 to 2008. It was once well above 10% and is now closer to 6%, per Mauboussin & Callahan, "Alpha and the Paradox of Skill". These figures are from secondary summaries. — [Institutional Investor](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/2bsu8copm52a2xoxxejnk/culture/five-questions-mauboussin-explores-why-luck-matters-to-investors); [Daily Economy](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/why-passive-management-wins-again/); [Morgan Stanley IM, "Dispersion and Alpha Conversion"](https://www.morganstanley.com/im/publication/insights/articles/dispersion-and-alpha-conversion.pdf)
- Mauboussin & Arbesman (2010) studied 5,593 large-cap U.S. active funds from 1962 to 2008 and tested them against 10,000 no-skill simulations. Actual results: 454 streaks of outperformance of at least 5 years, 3 of at least 10 years, and a longest streak of 15 years. That is more than chance predicts, so some skill exists, but it is rare. — [CXO Advisory](https://www.cxoadvisory.com/investing-expertise/outperformance-streaks-and-mutual-fund-manager-skill)
- Damodaran's heuristic: beating the market by 2–3% a year for 15 years with low variability suggests skill. The same average with high variability does not. — [Damodaran Substack](https://aswathdamodaran.substack.com/p/luck-versus-skill-how-can-you-tell-11-03-12)
- Fama–French estimate the standard deviation of *true* alpha across funds at only about 1.25% a year. That is small relative to noise. — cited in [Scribd doc](https://www.scribd.com/document/482122040/document-805456950-pdf) (secondary)

`case_study:hermes-lvmh-2009-2025` · tickers EU-RMS, EU-MC · confidence: single-source

From the 2009 trough, both compounded on Chinese wealth creation, price increases above inflation and supply-limited products (Birkin waitlists; Louis Vuitton never discounts). Hermès: ~€90 (2009) [unverified] -> ~€2,750 (Feb 2025) ≈ 30x; operating margin ~40%. LVMH: ~€40 (Mar 2009) [unverified] -> ~€900 (Apr 2023) ≈ 22x; Bernard Arnault briefly became world's richest. Split: mostly EPS (sales and margins up), plus P/E expansion to ~50x for Hermès and ~25-30x for LVMH [approx]. Side story: LVMH secretly built a ~17-23% Hermès stake via equity swaps (2010), fined by the AMF and distributed in 2014 — Hermès family formed a holding to lock control [from memory, unverified]. Reversal: May 2023 one-day $30bn luxury sell-off on US/China demand fears; China reopening bet faded; 2024 was a bad year for LVMH/Kering (Hermès held up); by Sept 2026 LVMH ~-55% from its 2023 peak (~-37% in 2026), out of Europe's top 10; Hermès down to ~€1,382 from ~€2,750 (date of quote unverified). EARLY SIGNAL visible ~2009-12: double-digit organic growth in Asia, price increases without volume loss, waitlists — pricing power. Who caught it: family owners (Arnault, Dumas/Puech); no documented outside name. LESSON: premiumisation compounders still carry demand cycles; Hermès (scarcity) held far better than LVMH (breadth) when the China aspirational buyer retreated, and a 50x P/E leaves no cushion.

- **Start → end:** Hermès ~€90; LVMH ~€40 (2009) [unverified] → Hermès ~€2,750 (Feb 2025); LVMH ~€900 (Apr 2023) (Hermès ~30x; LVMH ~22x)
- **EPS vs rerating:** mostly EPS + P/E expansion
- **Max drawdown:** LVMH ~-55% (2023-26); Hermès ~-50% (2025-26) [date unverified]
- **Early signal:** price hikes w/o volume loss, waitlists, Asian organic growth
- **Who caught it:** family owners
- **Ended/stalled:** LVMH 2023, Hermès 2025 peaks
- **Lesson:** scarcity beats breadth in luxury downturns; luxury is still cyclical
- **Sources:** [1](https://www.modaes.com/global/companies/lvmh-loses-market-value-and-falls-out-of-the-top-ten-in-europe-as-the-luxury-market-slows) · [2](https://en.ilsole24ore.com/art/lvmh-and-kering-are-far-from-their-highs-of-recent-years-AJlsw2EB) · [3](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-05-23/luxury-stocks-take-30-billion-hit-as-lvmh-hermes-lead-slump) · [4](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-06-04/the-big-china-play-that-fueled-luxury-stocks-is-now-fizzling-out) · [5](https://businessinsider.nl/this-chart-shows-what-a-bad-year-2024-was-for-luxury)

Mumbai investor behind Param Capital. Public holdings (>1% stakes): ~72-73 stocks as of early 2026; portfolio value estimates range from ~Rs 6,163 crore to ~Rs 7,373 crore depending on date and source. Largest disclosed holdings in Dec 2025 data: Neuland Laboratories (~Rs 496.5 crore) and Radico Khaitan (~Rs 379.4 crore). Q1 FY26 fresh buys included Valor Estate (6.5m shares, ~Rs 120.6 crore), J&K Bank, Wendt India, Tatva Chintan and Yatharth Hospital. Sector spread: pharma/CDMO, infrastructure, chemicals, textiles, alcobev. Edge: structural - large capital spread across many mid/small names, ability to take block and pre-IPO/QIP allocations; process (as reported) - blends earnings-growth/turnaround picks with momentum, actively adds and exits. Track record: no published return series; net-worth figures in media are aggregator estimates (single-source). Mistakes: specific losses are not documented in sources found; like other superstar books, many small positions have suffered 40-60% falls in smallcap drawdowns. Copyable: his top holdings illustrate a useful pattern - turnarounds that became re-rated compounders (Neuland's CDMO shift, Radico's premiumisation) - but the quarterly-lagged, >1%-only disclosure makes ticker-cloning unreliable.

`strategy:jain-valuation-contrarian` | confidence: **verified** | tags: india, process, contrarian, value

Approach (from interviews and fund behaviour): (1) Stay anchored to normalised earnings and valuations; refuse to pay bubble multiples (tech 1999-2000, realty 2007, quality-consumer at extreme P/Es). (2) Accept underperformance during bubbles - 'when you avoid certain bubbles, the returns take a hit.' (3) Overweight unloved large caps when they trade well below history, typically financials, energy, power and capital goods, and hold for multi-year mean reversion. (4) Low turnover, long horizon. Results: ~20% CAGR over ~20 years vs ~10% for the Nifty, with painful stretches (2013, 2015, 2018-20). Lesson from the PSU-heavy phase: cheapness without a catalyst (earnings upgrade, capex cycle, bad-loan clean-up) can last years and cause investor redemptions; for an individual, size contrarian large-cap bets so you can wait, and define the catalyst you're waiting for.
